notes: \cpara{Opens in the formal room where Jeffreyssai receives outsiders. In the book's order this is the first appearance of Jeffreyssai, the ``beisutsukai'' and the Conspiracies, although the author had introduced them in stories posted earlier, such as ``The Failures of Eld Science'' (May 2008). A reader of the book meets these names here without explanation.}
\cpara{Says the room is what outsiders expect of a ``Bayesian Master,'' and that he enjoys leaving them to their expectation.}
\cpara{Introduces the guest, on the business of ``her Conspiracy,'' dressed for it.}
\cpara{Her reply states the story's first principle: an expert's advice can move his opinion without being certain.}
\cpara{He asks how she knows the rules without formal training.}
\cpara{He winces at the idea of learning rationality by listening to people talk about it.}
\cpara{She separates trying to be a rationalist from trying to win an argument with one.}
\cpara{A reflection on the sunlight: the Sun will burn out, but that it shines now can never change, so a wish for permanence is already granted, and only change allows progress or loss.}
\cpara{He notes her record: her counsel has always been good. Her advice counts as evidence by its record as well as by her expertise.}
\cpara{He asks again, ``Only because I want to know the answer.''}
\cpara{She begins a statistic (985 cases in 1,000) and breaks off.}

\cpara{She admits the statistic was a joke and that only he can decide, but says he should hold his ritual for ``abandoning a long-held premise of your existence.'' What the premise is, the story does not say.}
\cpara{He accepts that an expert's judgment that he is ``probably wrong'' is reason enough to hold the ritual.}
\cpara{He concedes, with a finality meant to end the argument.}
\cpara{She takes a formal leave: a kiss on his hand and ``Farewell, sensei.''}
\cpara{He notices that ``farewell'' is a larger parting than ``goodbye,'' and invites her back.}
\cpara{She leaves with ``It won't be the same,'' and does not explain.}
\cpara{From here on, his actions are ``prescribed'': the ritual begins.}
\cpara{He cancels the next day's classes, promising his students a test.}

\cpara{The day before: idle reading and wandering, while he blocks every thought he has had before and every conclusion. This acts out the advice of ``Crisis of Faith,'' posted the day before: rest the previous day, and ``Clear your mind of all standard arguments.''}
\cpara{He keeps his mind idle without effort, a skill the story says long practice perfected.}
\cpara{In the morning he keeps hold of his dreams' chaos and goes down to the plainest room in the house.}

\cpara{The plaques carry three maxims, unattributed: P. C. Hodgell's ``That which can be destroyed by the truth should be,'' Gendlin's ``People can stand what is true, for they are already enduring it,'' and ``Curiosity seeks to annihilate itself,'' from the author's ``Twelve Virtues of Rationality.'' For the settings the first two came from, see the notes on ``You Can Face Reality.''}

\cpara{The tally: two changes of mind in seven sessions. The story treats the five kept beliefs as a normal result, so a belief kept after the ritual is not by itself a failed doubt. (``Crisis of Faith'' counted Aumann's kept faith as a failure because it took the faith to be false.) An empty plus column would show a missing ability, the story adds, unless you were ``born knowing the truth.''}
\cpara{He sits facing the blank wall, away from the plaques, to avoid distraction.}
\cpara{He rehearses mnemonics for ``seven major principles and sixty-two specific techniques,'' and for his own ``fourteen most embarrassing oversights.'' None of them is named.}
\cpara{The story ends as the crisis begins. It does not say what the question is, what he concludes, or in which column the mark goes. So it shows how the ritual is prepared, not what it achieves.}
